mcqs.question: Which statement correctly defines a thermodynamic system?

options.A: The part of the universe that is being studied, while everything else is the surroundings.
options.B: The entire universe, including all possible reactions.
options.C: Only the solid phase present in a reaction mixture.
options.D: The container holding the reactants, irrespective of what is studied.

mcqs.answer: The part of the universe that is being studied, while everything else is the surroundings.
mcqs.explanation: A thermodynamic system is the specific portion of the universe selected for analysis. Everything outside this portion is called the surroundings. Option A captures this definition. Option B describes the whole universe, not a system. Option C limits the system to a solid phase, which is incorrect. Option D confuses the container with the system; the container may be part of the surroundings if not under study.

mcqs.question: In the context of thermodynamics, the surroundings are best described as:

options.A: The portion of the universe that is under investigation.
options.B: The region that exchanges heat and work with the system.
options.C: Everything external to the system that can affect or be affected by the system.
options.D: Only the air surrounding the laboratory.

mcqs.answer: Everything external to the system that can affect or be affected by the system.
mcqs.explanation: Surroundings comprise everything outside the chosen system that can interact with it by exchanging heat, work, or matter. Option C states this comprehensively. Option A actually defines the system. Option B describes only the part of the surroundings that participates in energy exchange, not the whole surroundings. Option D is too narrow, limiting surroundings to laboratory air.

mcqs.learning_point: Distinguish open, closed and isolated systems
mcqs.question: Which of the following correctly distinguishes open, closed and isolated systems?

options.A: In an open system, both matter and energy can cross the boundary; in a closed system, only energy can cross; in an isolated system, neither matter nor energy can cross.
options.B: In an open system, only energy can cross; in a closed system, both matter and energy can cross; in an isolated system, only matter can cross.
options.C: In an open system, neither matter nor energy can cross; in a closed system, only matter can cross; in an isolated system, both can cross.
options.D: In an open system, only matter can cross; in a closed system, only energy can cross; in an isolated system, both can cross.

mcqs.answer: In an open system, both matter and energy can cross the boundary; in a closed system, only energy can cross; in an isolated system, neither matter nor energy can cross.
mcqs.explanation: Open systems exchange both matter and energy with surroundings. Closed systems allow energy (heat or work) exchange but no matter transfer. Isolated systems exchange neither matter nor energy. Option A states these definitions accurately. The other options mix up the allowed exchanges, leading to incorrect classifications.

mcqs.question: Which type of boundary permits the exchange of energy (heat or work) but prevents any matter from crossing between the system and its surroundings?

options.A: A rigid, impermeable boundary that does not allow heat transfer.
options.B: A flexible, permeable boundary that allows both matter and energy exchange.
options.C: A rigid, impermeable (diathermal) boundary that allows heat transfer but blocks matter.
options.D: A flexible, impermeable boundary that allows work exchange but not heat.

mcqs.answer: A rigid, impermeable (diathermal) boundary that allows heat transfer but blocks matter.
mcqs.explanation: A boundary that is impermeable to matter but diathermal (allows heat) enables energy exchange while preventing matter transfer; this matches the description in option C. Option A blocks both heat and matter, so it does not allow energy exchange. Option B allows matter, contradicting the requirement. Option D mentions work exchange without heat, which is not the typical definition of a diathermal boundary.
